newsitem.title: CHINA: FEATURE - Who owns this thriving Shanghai paint factory?.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Who owns this thriving Shanghai paint factory?.

text.p: The workers and managers of the Shanghai Hua Shen Chemical factory built the firm from nothing without using a cent of state money.
The question now is: who owns it?
A lot is at stake. The company has net assets worth 800 million yuan ($96.4 million), an average of 1.38 million yuan for each of its 580 staff.

Some of the company's staff want to turn the factory, which makes paint, into a shareholding company, but the factory chief believes it is better off maintaining its status as a "collectively owned enterprise".

The debate over who owns what is intensifying as China transforms its economy from one where the state owned everything to one with growing numbers of companies that are privately-owned or have shares in private hands.
Hua Shen was set up in 1982 as a "collective". Its capital came from the people who set it up, but they were not given shares.
The following year, they received the money back and the status of the firm's ownership has not changed since.

China has tens of thousands of factories and other firms which are referred to as "collectively owned", especially the township enterprises of East China, which are "owned" by the towns and villages in which they exist.
There is no known case of the ownership of a so-called "collectively owned enterprise" being transferred to the residents of a township or to the enterprise's workers.
OUTPUT, SALES AND PROFITS ON THE RISE

Hua Shen officials put 1996 paint output at 100,000 tonnes, with sales of 1.45 billion yuan and profits of 350 million, up from 60,000 tonnes, 1.12 billion yuan and 200 million in 1995. The company has substantial bank savings and no debt, they say.
They say its products, for use in homes, hotels, restaurants and furniture, hold a 30 percent national market share for the paints in some product categories.
At a time when the government is encouraging the establishment of shareholding companies, the question is who owns the Hua Shen assets and what is the appropriate form of this ownership?

"These assets all belong to us, the collective," said vice factory director Ye Zhengde. "We have had no fund allocation or investment from the state and no investment from any other economic organisation. We built up this firm by ourselves."
Since 1995, some workers and management have started to consider turning the firm into a shareholding company.

"How to do this has not been decided yet," said Le Guoqing, another vice director. "There is the problem of who the assets belong to. After this is decided by a government department, we can consider what to do.
"If the evaluation finds the assets belong to the government, we cannot become a shareholding firm," he said.
Factory chief Li Longming says the best solution is to continue with the "collective ownership" phraseology. He opposes dividing the firm into shares and giving them to the workers.
"If everyone wants to take their money out, what would we do? Is it not better to concentrate the money, reinvest, raise profits and increase worker incomes?" he said.
GOOD WAGES, CHEAP HOUSING
Li said his workers would this year take home on average 40,000 yuan in wages and bonuses, up from 32,000 in 1995, more than three times the average Shanghai wage.
Each worker has an apartment provided by the company, with a subsidised rent of 10-20 yuan a month. The accommodation becomes their own property after 10 years, he said.
The company wants to maintain its rapid pace of expansion and reach sales of six billion yuan by the year 2000, he said.

Since the 1980s, Beijing has encouraged the setting up of shareholding companies as a more efficient alternative to those directly run by the state. But most of the shares are owned by state units even if the firms are run independently.
Hua Shen was born in March 1982 when Li Longming used 2,000 yuan of his own money to buy three vats and other equipment and with nine workers began processing paint in a shed in a Shanghai suburb.
Capitalising on the inability of state firms to respond to a changing market, the company developed its own equipment and products mainly aimed at domestic users and makers of furniture.
Ye recalled that theirs was the first paint factory to produce 0.5 kg cans of paint, aimed at individual users, at a time when state firms only turned out large-volume cans.

Company officials attribute the rapid growth of the company to its adaptability to the market, a standard of equipment equal to that in foreign countries and the high motivation of its workers, who earn unusually high wages and obtain cheap housing.
